title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Extensions: Extension Definitions
subtitle: Six optional add-ons that let a TLS client tell a server which site it wants, and ask for less work on small devices.
summary: RFC 6066 defines six extensions for Transport Layer Security 1.2: server_name, max_fragment_length, client_certificate_url, trusted_ca_keys, truncated_hmac and status_request. Each rides inside the client and server hello messages, so a client that knows an extension can still talk to a server that does not. The best known is Server Name Indication, which lets one address host many secure sites. The rest mostly help constrained devices save memory and bandwidth.

eli5.summary: When you phone a big office building, you can say which person you want before anyone answers. These extensions are polite extra requests in the first message of a secure chat, like "which site do you want?" or "please use short messages, my memory is small".

tldr.problem: TLS 1.2 had a way to add extensions but defined almost none, so clients could not say which site they wanted or ask for savings on small devices.
tldr.mechanism: Six extension types, numbered 0 to 5, are carried in the client hello. A server that supports one answers in its server hello, or ignores it.
tldr.outcome: Server Name Indication became part of almost every HTTPS connection, and OCSP stapling through status_request is widely used. Later specifications updated this RFC, for example RFC 8449 adds a Record Size Limit extension.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246) built a framework for extensions into the handshake, and it also describes how new extension code points are allocated. But it defines only one extension itself, Signature Algorithms. RFC 6066 supplies the rest of the practical ones that were already deployed, adapted "for the most part" from RFC 4366, which had covered TLS 1.0 and 1.1.

All six extensions are designed to be backwards compatible. A client that supports them can talk to a server that does not, and the reverse. Two other rules apply to all of them. Any extension messages sent during the handshake MUST be included in the hash calculations for the Finished messages. And the extensions matter only when a session starts: if a client asks to resume an old session, the server MUST ignore them and send a server hello with none of the extension types, and the settings from the original session carry over.

Backward compatible
Old clients and old servers simply never see or answer the new extensions.
Negotiated, not imposed
The client offers in its hello; the server accepts by echoing the extension in its hello.
Handshake only
On a resumed session the server ignores the extensions and the earlier results continue to apply.
sections.eli5: The first message of a secure chat has room for extra sticky notes. A new computer can attach notes; an old computer just doesn't read them and the chat still works.

sections.title: Why these extensions exist
sections.content:
Each extension answers one practical problem. Hosting many sites on one network address meant a server could not tell which certificate to present before it had to present one. Some clients, such as small embedded devices, have limited memory or sit on slow access networks. The RFC lists these goals one by one: tell the server the name being contacted, negotiate a smaller maximum fragment length, send a certificate URL instead of a certificate, say which CA root keys the client holds, use shorter MAC tags, and receive certificate status in the handshake so a Certificate Revocation List does not need to be downloaded.

The table summarises the six, with the extension type number each one uses on the wire.
sections.eli5: Some computers are tiny and forgetful, and one big computer can pretend to be many websites. These extras fix both problems.

sections.title: Handshake changes and error alerts
sections.content:
Section 2 of the RFC adds two new handshake message types to the TLS handshake structure: certificate_url(21) and certificate_status(22). They carry the CertificateURL and CertificateStatus messages described below.

Section 9 adds four new alerts, numbered 111 to 114. To avoid breaking existing clients and servers, they MUST NOT be sent unless the sender has received an extended hello from the other party.

Unrecognised names are a policy choice. If the server understood the extension but not the name, it SHOULD either send a fatal unrecognized_name(112) alert or carry on. A warning-level alert is NOT RECOMMENDED because client behaviour on warnings is unpredictable.
sections.eli5: Two new kinds of message and four new "uh-oh" signals were added, but they are only used between computers that already said they understand extensions.

sections.title: Server Name Indication
sections.content:
TLS originally had no way for a client to say which server name it was trying to reach. For a host running several virtual servers behind one address, that matters before any certificate is sent. A client MAY therefore include a server_name extension (type 0) whose data is a ServerNameList. Each entry is a name_type, of which only host_name(0) is defined, followed by a HostName: a fully qualified DNS name in ASCII, without a trailing dot, with a 16-bit length in front. Internationalised names use their A-label form. Literal IPv4 and IPv6 addresses are not permitted.

The list MUST NOT contain more than one name of the same type. A server that uses the name to pick a certificate puts an empty server_name extension in its server hello. When deciding whether to resume a session, the server MUST NOT accept resumption if the name differs from the original one. The client SHOULD send the same name on resumption.

The name is sent in the clear in the client hello, so anyone watching the network can read it. This RFC does not address that.
sections.eli5: Before the big building opens its door, you say "I'm here to see Ms. Smith." Now the guard can hand you Ms. Smith's badge, not someone else's.

sections.title: Smaller messages and fewer certificates
sections.content:
Four extensions help constrained clients. max_fragment_length (type 1) lets a client ask for a plaintext fragment limit of 2^9, 2^10, 2^11 or 2^12 bytes instead of the default 2^14. The server agrees by echoing the same value; any other value, or a reply that differs from the request, MUST abort the handshake with illegal_parameter. Fragmenting starts immediately, including for handshake messages.

client_certificate_url (type 2) lets a client send a CertificateURL message listing URLs and SHA-1 hashes instead of the certificates. The server fetches each one, MUST support the http scheme, MUST NOT follow redirects, and MUST abort with bad_certificate_hash_value(114) if a hash does not match. The one-byte padding field MUST be 0x01.

trusted_ca_keys (type 3) lets a client list the CA root keys it holds, by pre_agreed, key SHA-1 hash, X.509 name or certificate SHA-1 hash. truncated_hmac (type 4) cuts MAC tags to 80 bits, so only the first 10 bytes of the HMAC output are sent and checked.
sections.eli5: A small phone can say "please send me short messages", "here's a link to my ID instead of the ID itself", "I only know these few official stamps", and "you can shorten the secret handshake code".

sections.title: Certificate status request
sections.content:
The status_request extension (type 5) lets a client ask the server to include proof that its certificate has not been revoked, so the client does not have to download a Certificate Revocation List or make its own OCSP query. The client sends a CertificateStatusRequest. The only status type defined is ocsp(1), holding a list of OCSP responder IDs the client trusts and optional request extensions. An empty responder list means the server already knows which responders to use.

The server replies with an empty status_request extension in its hello and, right after the Certificate message and before any ServerKeyExchange or CertificateRequest, may send a CertificateStatus message holding one complete DER-encoded OCSP response of up to 2^24-1 bytes. It MUST NOT send that message unless it received and echoed the extension, and it MAY still choose not to send one. A client that gets a response it is not happy with MUST abort with bad_certificate_status_response(113).
sections.eli5: Instead of calling the police station to check that an ID card was not cancelled, you ask the person to hand you a freshly stamped note that says it is still good.

sections.title: Security considerations
sections.content:
Each extension has its own notes. For server_name, implementations MUST ensure that a buffer overflow does not occur whatever the length fields say. Application servers that rely on the name in the application protocol matching the TLS name MUST check that the client did not present a different one.

The biggest risk is client_certificate_url: the server becomes a client of arbitrary URLs that an attacker supplies. That can be used to attack other hosts, to flood a target, or to probe hosts behind the server's firewall. The RFC RECOMMENDS that the extension be switched on specifically by an administrator, with only a minimal set of URI schemes enabled. SHA-1 is still used for the hashes, and the RFC argues that second pre-image resistance, not collision resistance, is what matters there.

For status_request, an attacker with a stolen key could simply pretend not to support the extension, so a client that must have revocation checking SHOULD either query OCSP directly or abort the handshake.
sections.eli5: The scariest sticky note is "go look at this link for me", because a trickster could point the helper at somewhere it should never go. So that one stays off unless the grown-up turns it on.

data.title: New code points (Sections 2 and 9)
data.code:
HandshakeType
  certificate_url(21)
  certificate_status(22)

AlertDescription
  certificate_unobtainable(111)
  unrecognized_name(112)
  bad_certificate_status_response(113)
  bad_certificate_hash_value(114)

fields.name: ServerNameList length
fields.desc: Length of the server_name_list vector in bytes (a 16-bit length prefix, 1 to 2^16-1).

fields.name: name_type
fields.desc: host_name(0) is the only name type defined.

fields.name: HostName length
fields.desc: Length of the HostName vector in bytes; every future name type also begins with a 16-bit length.

fields.name: HostName
fields.desc: ASCII DNS name without a trailing dot. Shown here as 11 bytes for the example name; the real field is variable length.

items.title: max_fragment_length (1)
items.text: Values 1 to 4 mean 2^9, 2^10, 2^11 or 2^12 bytes. At 2^9 the record layer output is at most 805 bytes with the cipher suites known at the time.

items.title: client_certificate_url (2)
items.text: CertificateURL is a CertChainType (individual_certs or pkipath) and a list of URL, 0x01 padding byte, and 20-byte SHA-1 hash.

items.title: trusted_ca_keys (3)
items.text: Identifier types pre_agreed(0), key_sha1_hash(1), x509_name(2), cert_sha1_hash(3).

items.title: truncated_hmac (4)
items.text: Empty extension data. mac_length becomes 10 bytes; the pseudo-random function is not affected.

messages.label: ClientHello + status_request (ocsp)
messages.note: Optionally with server_name and other extensions.

messages.label: ServerHello + status_request (empty)
messages.note: Required if the server will send CertificateStatus.

messages.label: CertificateStatus (certificate_status, 22)
messages.note: Holds one DER-encoded OCSP response. Comes immediately after Certificate.

TLS 1.3 updates this RFC; Record Size Limit extension appears

today: Server Name Indication is in practice part of nearly every HTTPS connection: browsers and common libraries send it, and web servers and content delivery networks use it to choose a certificate. OCSP stapling uses the status_request extension. Later specifications built on this RFC. RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3) and RFC 8449 (Record Size Limit Extension) are both listed in the RFC index as updating it, as is RFC 9325 (BCP 195 recommendations for secure use of TLS and DTLS).

implementations.name: OpenSSL
implementations.note: Supports server_name and status_request in its TLS stack.

implementations.name: Wireshark
implementations.note: Decodes TLS extensions, including server_name, in captured client hellos.
